list.listitem: Low-risk women should take 0.4 mg of folic acid daily for at least 1 month prior to conception to reduce the rate of neural tube defects (NTDs) by 70%; high-risk women should take 4 mg of folic acid daily for at least 1 month prior to conception.A

For prenatal screening, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG, 2017) and the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SOGC, 2021) recommend routine sonographic anatomical screening for all pregnant women in the second trimester.B

If unable to perform second-trimester anatomical sonography due to geographic location or clinical factors (e.g., body mass index >35 kg/m2), offer maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP) testing to all pregnant women between 16 and 18 weeks' gestation. Assure accurate dating for all women with abnormal results, with consideration of redrawing the serum test if the dates are inaccurate.B

If the MSAFP is positive, refer for either high-resolution targeted fetal ultrasound or amniocentesis for measurement of amniotic fluid levels of alpha-fetoprotein and acetylcholinesterase if the proper ultrasound equipment and expertise are unavailable. If chromosome analysis is necessary, amniocentesis is preferred.B

ACOG (2017) recommends genetic evaluation by amniocentesis for chromosomal microarray following identification of an NTD if the patient wishes to continue the pregnancy because identification of a genetic abnormality in a fetus with an NTD has implications for counseling regarding prognosis, pregnancy management, and determining whether the patient is a candidate for in utero NTD repair.B SOGC (2021) recommends genetic evaluation if a diagnostic amniocentesis is performed. Otherwise, consider fetal exome sequencing for fetuses with myelomeningocele or other spina bifida anomalies after multidisciplinary counseling and if appropriate criteria for molecular genetic sequencing are met.
Fetuses with confirmed NTDs should be delivered in a center capable of handling all aspects of treatment and potential neonatal complications in a child with a NTD.B

Based on a single trial, prenatal versus postnatal repair of myelomeningocele results in better infant outcomes but with greater risk of preterm delivery and uterine rupture (estimated at 11-14%) at delivery.B

background.definition: A neural tube defect (NTD), also known as dysraphism, is a congenital anomaly of the central nervous system. The major NTDs are shown in and are described by their anatomical location and neural content. The primary structural malformation affects the spine and/or cranium. Outcomes and disabilities depend on the level and extent of the lesion.

list.listitem: 0.29 per 1000 of all live births in the United States in 2005. The Center for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that 3,000 pregnancies in the U.S. are affected by NTDs annually.
0.31 per 1000 live Hispanic births, 0.26 per 1000 live black births, and 0.29 per 1000 live non-Hispanic white births in the United States in 2005.
Cases of NTD appear to be highest in Ireland, the US and the UK, and lowest in Japan.
Global incidence of anencephaly is estimated at 8.3 per 10,000 births (95% CI 5.5-9.9 per 10,000 births).
Prevalence of NTDs has decreased due to the required folic acid fortification of grain products in the United States in 1998.

Prevalence of spina bifida for 1995 to 1996 was 0.51 per 1000 live births in the United States and decreased to 0.34 per 1000 live births for the period between 1999 and 2000. Rates of anencephaly decreased from 0.25 per 1,000 to 0.21 per 1000 over the same years.

Data from 2004-2006 showed prevalence rates of spina bifida of 0.34 per 1000 live births and 0.44 per 1000 live births, still births or terminations. For anencephaly, prevalence rates were 0.06 per 1000 live births and 0.25 per 1000 live births, still births or terminations.

Global prevalence of NTDs is 2 per 1000 births or approximately 214,000-322,000 affected pregnancies annually worldwide. Global prevalence of anencephaly is estimated at 5.1 per 10,000 births (95% CI 4.7-5.5 per 10,000 births).

European data show no change in prevalence of NTD (pooled prevalence 9.1 per 10,000 births) since an initial decrease of 3% per year observed in 1999-2003; live birth prevalence of NTD generally decreased, especially for anencephaly.

Based on data from the US National Spina Bifida Patient Registry of 2172 patient first visits, the mean age was 10.1 years and more patients had mid-low lumbar lesions (44.8%) than sacral (33%) or high lumbar and thoracic lesions (24.9%). The most common surgery was ventricular shunt placement (65.7%) and most patients managed their bladder impairment with intermittent catheterization (69.0%).
The estimated total lifetime direct cost of care for a child born with spina bifida in the US is $791,900.

Among 7776 patients with spina bifida who were hospitalized, the 3888 patients who had pressure injuries had an increased length of stay of 1.2 days and an average excess cost of $1182 compared to a matched group of 3888 patients without pressure injuries.
NTD is the second-most-common major congenital anomaly.

In addition to a reduction in NTDs, peri-conception folic acid supplementation is associated with decreased risks of low birth weight and SGA and may reduce childhood behavioral problems. In a matched case-cohort study, fetuses with isolated NTDs compared to those without any congenital anomalies were more likely to have abnormal placental pathology including single umbilical artery, many Hofbauer cells and stromal fibrosis which may explain some of these risks.

Presence of an NTD increases risk of stillbirth of that fetus. In one study, estimated risk was 24/1000 (95% CI 17-34) compared to 6/1000 US stillbirth rate overall. Risk may be underestimated without accounting for elective termination.

Lack of folic acid intake, vitamin B12 deficiency, opiod use during pregnancy, maternal anticonvulsant drugs, maternal obesity, maternal hyperthermia, and diabetes all adversely affect neural tube development.
Chromosomal abnormalities including trisomy 13 and 18.

A genetic predisposition exists, with a risk of recurrence of 3% to 4% after 1 child is born with an NTD and 10% if more than 1 child is born with an NTD to the same mother. Mutations in the planar cell polarity gene VANGL1 and FZD6 are associated with NTDs.
MTRR A66G and MTHFR 677 C > T gene polymorphisms are associated with maternal risk for NTD.
NTDs result from a failure of induction of overlying ectoderm from the primitive endoderm in the third week of development after conception, resulting in the lack of spontaneous closure of the CNS.
Genomic instability or lack of DNA repair pathways, linked to folate deficiency, has been implicated in risk of development of NTDs.

Retinoic acid receptor (RAR) signaling malfunctions have been observed in human NTDs. Investigators in one study found significant upregulation of retinoic acid receptor γ (RARγ) mRNA in the brain tissues of human fetuses with anencephaly.

Functional changes associated with NTDs, depending on the level and severity of the defect, include infectious complications, paraplegia, bladder and bowel incontinence, Arnold-Chiari malformations (both the cerebellum and brain stem extend into the foramen magnum), hydrocephalus, and diminished intelligence (if hydrocephalus is present).

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: History of previous affected pregnancy, same partner
Inadequate maternal intake of folic acid
Use of nitrosatable drugs (e.g., chlordiazepoxide, nitrofurantoin, and chlorpheniramine) (anencephalic births)
Maternal fever during first trimester pregnancy
Maternal influenza during first trimester pregnancy
Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (8% had neuraxial abnormalities)
Opioid analgesics during early pregnancy (spina bifida)
Paternal exposure to agent orange (spina bifida)

list.listitem: Give folic acid 4 mg/day beginning at least 1 to 3 months prior to conception and continuing through the first trimester for women planning pregnancy who have previously had a pregnancy affected by a NTD to reduce the risk of recurrence.A

The USPSTF (2023) recommends that all women planning pregnancy should take a daily multivitamin containing 0.4 to 0.8 mg of folic acid beginning at least 1 month prior to conception and continuing through the first trimester (NNT = 847 to prevent 1 NTD).A Consider continuing folic acid throughout the entire pregnancy and as long as breastfeeding continues at a dose of 0.4 (low-risk women) to 1 mg (moderate to high-risk women).

ACOG (2017) and SOGC (2021) recommend routine sonographic prenatal screening be offered to all pregnant women in the second trimester between 18- and 22-weeks gestation to maximize testing accuracy, achieve low false-positive rates, and allow optimal management of affected pregnancies.B They also recommend first-trimester sonographic NTD screening, especially for women with moderate- or high-risk factors.
Screen for NTD by measuring MSAFP between 16 and 18 weeks' gestation. Risk of NTD 9s 2% if MSAFP is elevated at 2.5 multiples of the mean.B
Maternal serum cell-free placental DNA can also be used for aneuploidy screening.A
In a 3-year retrospective study of fetal anomaly ultrasound scans in the UK, fetal scans detection rates were 96.3% for anencephaly (95% CI 81.7-99.3%) and 93.8% for spina bifida (95% CI 91.8-95.3%).

ACOG (2017) and SOGC (2021) support a pre-conception/inter-pregnancy diet that is high in folate and 0.4 mg of folic acid for low-risk women considering pregnancy. The USPSTF (2023) recommends a daily supplement of 0.4 mg to 0.8 mg folic acid for all persons who plan to or could become pregnant. SOGC recommends higher doses of 1 mg of folic acid for women at moderate risk of NTD (risk factors including personal or family history of other folic acid-sensitive anomalies, family history of NTD in first or second degree relative, diabetes, use of teratogenic medications or gastrointestinal malabsorption) and 4 mg of folic acid for women with a personal or partner history of NTD or a previous pregnancy affected by an NTD.

Authors of a global systematic review and meta-analysis found lower period prevalence of spina bifida among live births in geographical regions with mandatory versus voluntary folic acid fortification (33.86 per 100,000 vs. 48.35 per 100,000).

Cochrane authors found a reduction in NTD for women taking daily folic acid supplementation compared with placebo or vitamins and minerals without folic acid (risk ratio (RR) 0.31; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.17-0.58) based on five studies with 6708 births.

Using 6 population databases from before and after mandatory folic acid fortification in the US, spina bifida prevalence declined by 23% (prevalence ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.71-0.85) and case severity decreased by 70% (aOR 0.30, 95% CI 0.26-0.35).

The updated 2023 evidence report for the United States Preventive Services Task Force confirms benefit based on additional observational studies. The odds ratio (OR) for the single RCT was 0.13 (95% CI, 0.03-0.65). One new cohort study reported a statistically significant reduced risk of NTDs associated with folic acid supplementation taken before pregnancy (aRR 0.54, 95% CI 0.31-0.91), during pregnancy (aRR 0.62, 95% CI 0.39-0.97), and before and during pregnancy (aRR 0.49, 95% CI 0.29-0.83) for 2 of 3 time periods studied and no significant harms.

In a multicenter prospective study of 17,713 women, those taking the recommended dosage of 0.4 or 0.8 mg/day of folic acid perinatally compared to women without supplementation had a non-significant albeit lower risk of NTDs (7.0 vs. 11.5 per 10,000 infants; OR 0.6, 95% CI 0.1-5.2). However, the authors found that initiation of folic acid around 2 months prior to pregnancy with a duration of at least 4 months achieved the lowest risk of congenital malformations (primarily heart).

In an RCT of 119 mother-child pairs enrolled in the "Folic Acid Supplementation in the Second and Third Trimesters" trial, continued folic acid supplementation at 0.4 mg daily beyond 14 weeks gestation was of benefit on child neurocognitive development at 11 years of age. Specifically, compared with placebo, children who received continued supplementation as fetuses scored significantly higher in two Processing Speed tests and in Verbal Comprehension among girls.

Authors of a systematic review of 35 studies, including 4 RCTs, conducted in high-income countries examining the association between intake of 3 or more vitamins or minerals in tablets or capsules and adverse birth outcomes found a reduction in risk of NTDs (RR 0.67, 95% confidence interval, 0.52-0.87), cardiovascular and urinary tract defects and limb deficiencies. No studies compared multivitamins to folic acid and iron supplementation. Quality of evidence was low or very low for all outcomes except for NTD recurrence for which a moderate degree of clinical evidence was found.

In a discontinuation trial, patients with spina bifida on clean urinary catheterization had fewer urinary tract infections (UTIs) if they remained on prophylaxis (1 extra UTI for every 2 patients who discontinued low dose chemoprophylaxis for a year). Male gender and a low pre-study rate of UTI predicted success with discontinuation.

In a Turkish RCT of 37 paraplegic newborns with open NTDs undergoing surgical repair, the 19 randomized to topical rifampin and cefotaxime had no infectious complications compared to the group randomized to saline and cefotaxime for whom 3 had surgical site infection, 3 had urinary tract infection, and 5 had sepsis.
Adequate counseling and follow-up services should be available for women with abnormal sonography or serum test results (MSAFP>2.5 of the multiple of mean [MoM]).B
If MSAFP is 2.5 or more multiples of the mean, then a high-resolution targeted fetal ultrasound should be performed.B
Prenatal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be considered if further detailed assessment of the fetal central nervous system is required for diagnostic or management counseling.A
An amniocentesis measuring both alpha-fetoprotein and acetylcholinesterase in the amniotic fluid is an alternative if access to ultrasound and an appropriately trained ultrasonographer is lacking.B

The American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (2019) state that testing for MSAFP and acetylcholinesterase in amniotic fluid and/or identification of the lesion by targeted ultrasound is considered diagnostic of open NTDs.
Spinal bifida occulta may present with a hemangioma, port-wine stain, or a tuft of hair or sinus tract immediately above the gluteal fold.

Similarly, the hair tuft of the scalp and hair collar sign are associated with neurovascular anomalies; in one 10-year multicenter study, 56/78 patients underwent cranial and brain imaging of whom 23 (41%) had abnormal findings including cranial/bone defects with central nervous system communication and central nervous system abnormalities.
Meningoceles may present in addition to and beneath the above-described findings, with a fluctuant midline mass that may transilluminate.

Myelomeningoceles present with a sac-like cystic structure covered with a thin layer of partially epithelialized tissue. Cognitive defects are common in children with myelomeningocele related to the associated Arnold-Chiari malformation.

Urinary continence varies with lesion level and ventricular shunt presence. In one chart review study, the urinary continence rate was highest in patients with a tethered spinal cord (57%), lipomyelomeningocele (65%) or sacral myelomeningocele (60%) versus thoracic and lumbar myelomeningocele (25% and 26%, respectively); most patients (73%) were continent of feces, which did not vary with lesion level.

Authors of a systematic review identified 49 case reports or case series with 730 patients with tethered cord syndrome. The mean age was 36 years and patients had experienced symptoms for a mean of 4.7 years. The most common symptoms were pain (81%), motor deficits (63%), sensory deficits (61%), bladder dysfunction (56%) and bowel dysfunction (15%).

Another systematic review of controlled studies and case series found overall a low quality of literature. Surgical detethering was associated with improvement in neurologic status, but also was associated with CSF leakage.
Anencephaly presents a distinctive appearance with a large defect of the calvarium, meninges, and scalp associated with a rudimentary brain with absent cerebral hemispheres and cerebellum.
Among live births in the United States in 2005 with dysraphism (abnormal structure of the spine), 61.4% of them had meningocele or meningomyelocele and 38.6% had anencephaly.

If available, order a high-resolution targeted fetal ultrasound for any pregnant woman who has an MSAFP level equal to 2.5 MoM. The sensitivity of the test is 100% for NTDs. The study should be performed by an ultrasonographer with training in NTD detection.

Maternal serum α-fetoprotein variants L2 and L3 are favorable biomarkers of open NTDs with an area under the curve of 0.83 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.73-0.93) for AFP-L2 and 0.89 (95% CI 0.81-0.96) for AFP-L3. The optimal diagnostic thresholds were 1.47 MoM and 1.94 MoM, respectively. Investigations including use of homocysteine and combining complement factors with MSAFP to improve non-invasive prediction of NTDs are ongoing.

Measurement of the level of alpha-fetoprotein and acetylcholinesterase in amniotic fluid obtained from an amniocentesis is an alternative diagnostic tool for NTDs. These 2 diagnostic tests combine to detect 100% of open NTDs.

The American College of Radiology practice parameter report (2021) states that ultrasound of the infant spine, performed by an experienced sonography, is an accurate and cost-effective tool comparable to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for evaluating congenital or acquired abnormalities in neonates and young infants. Indications include lumbosacral stigmata of NTDs and suspected NTDs. ACR recommends MRI when an anomaly is visualized by ultrasound but the etiology remains uncertain.

In one retrospective case series of 151 infants with a sacral dimple, there was low yield of ultrasonography for detecting spinal dysraphism—of 151 infants, 20% had an abnormal spinal ultrasound of whom 7 (5%) had abnormal spinal MRI and 2 (1%) required neurosurgical intervention.
MRI is recommended if tethered cord is suspected based on a systematic review.
For diagnosis of UTI in children with tethered cord, pyuria was the most sensitive test (useful to rule out if negative) and nitrities the most specific (useful if positive).
If a pregnant woman has an elevated MSAFP (2.5 multiples of the mean or greater), then a high-resolution targeted ultrasound should be performed to search for an NTD.

If a high-resolution targeted ultrasound is not available, an alternative diagnostic tool is the presence of acetylcholinesterase in the amniotic fluid obtained from an amniocentesis. A combination of elevated level of serum alpha-fetoprotein and the presence of acetylcholinesterase in the amniotic fluid is diagnostic for an NTD.

A patient with a fetus with an NTD should be offered the management options of pregnancy termination, expectant management with neonatal surgical repair, and in utero fetal repair for appropriate candidates.

Genetic evaluation by amniocentesis for chromosomal microarray should be considered because the identification of a genetic abnormality in a fetus with an NTD has implications for counseling regarding prognosis, pregnancy management, and determining whether the patient is a candidate for in utero NTD repair.
Delivery should occur at a center capable of handling all aspects of treatment and potential complications.B

Optimal method of delivery in infants with NTD is unclear. ACOG recommends that decisions about the timing and route of delivery be made individually in consultation with personnel with experience and knowledge of NTDs.C
Children should be delivered at term unless ventriculomegaly necessitates delivery prior to term for the purposes of ventricular shunt placement.B
Surgical closure with shunting to prevent and/or treat hydrocephalus improves prognosis of open spina bifida.

Augmentation cystoplasty, usually with a detubularized patch of ileum, is used for medically refractory neurogenic bladder in patients with spina bifida; there is some concern about subsequent bladder malignancy.

A systematic review of 49 case reports and case series with 730 patients with Tethered Cord Syndrome reported that post-operatively, pain improved in 81%, motor symptoms in 61%, sensory symptoms in 45%, and bladder symptoms in 45%.
Prenatal vs.postnatal surgery (see also additional information in prognosis)

An RCT of prenatal versus postnatal repair of myelomeningocele in 158 patients was stopped early in favor of prenatal repair. This was based on improved composite rates of mortality or need for CSF shunt at 12 months (68% of infants in the prenatal-surgery group vs 98% of those in the postnatal-surgery group) and improved composite score for mental development and motor function at 30 months. Shunt placement was needed by 40% in the prenatal-surgery group and 82% in the postnatal-surgery group. Prenatal surgery, however, resulted in an increased risk of preterm delivery and uterine dehiscence at delivery.

In a subsequent report of risk factors for complications of prenatal surgery from this trial, earlier gestational age at surgery was associated with increased risk of spontaneous rupture of membranes (OR 1.49; 95% CI, 1.01-2.22) and oligohydramnios was associated with an increased risk of preterm delivery (OR 9.21; 95% CI, 2.19-38.78).

The prenatal surgery group in this study, however, had significantly lower negative family impact of caring for a child with spina bifida up to 30 months, based on the revised 15-item Impact on Family Scale scores, as well as lower familial-social impact subscale scores compared to the postnatal surgery group; parental stress reports were similar.

Authors of a systematic review of 27 nonrandomized studies of spina bifida repair over the 10-year period following the Management of Myelomeningocele Study Trial found prenatal surgery favored over postnatal surgery for rates of hydrocephalus (45.6% vs. 66.6%), reversal of hindbrain herniation (63.1% vs. 33.7%), and urinary continence (41.0% vs. 8.9%). However, overall, mortality was higher in prenatally-treated (0% to 8.4% for open and 7.0% to 20% for fetoscopic surgery) vs. postnatally-treated cases (0% to 3.3%).
Authors of a systematic review of 10 studies of repair of myelomeningocele found no significant increase in relative risk of tethered spinal cord between prenatal and postnatal closure.

In a case series of 9 fetuses with occipital encephalocele (OE) and microcephaly who underwent intrauterine OE repair at gestational ages of less than 27 weeks, all had microcephaly reversal and 3 patients required ventriculoperitoneal shunting by 1 year of life. In comparison with 12 patients who underwent postnatal repair, 10 of whom refused fetal surgery and 2 cases not meeting inclusion criteria for fetal surgery, neurocognitive development was much better, with median scores on the Bayley Scales of Infant Development II of 98.7 for the fetal surgery group vs. 27.8 for the postnatal repair group.

In a report from a single institution of 127 patients with open NTDs, 93 of whom underwent prenatal (51 fetoscopic and 42 open hysterotomy) and 34 postnatal repair, postnatally-repaired cases showed worse motor function at birth and at 12 months of age.

In a Canadian case series of 27 women whose fetuses underwent open myelomeningocele closure performed at the Ontario Fetal Centre at a mean gestational age of 25 + 0.7 weeks, no fetal deaths occurred but there were 3 infant deaths. All but 1 of 26 were delivered via cesarean section and maternal complications occurred in 9 women (34.6%). Of 14 surviving infants reaching at least 1 year of age, 5 have undergone ventriculo-peritoneal shunting. Of 9 infants who have not yet reached 1 year of age, 3 (33.3%) have undergone endoscopic third ventriculostomy but none underwent shunting.

Authors of a case series of 300 prenatal fetoscopic open spina bifida repairs completed at 23.6 + 1.4 weeks gestation and reported to the International Fetoscopic Neural Tube Defect Repair Consortium compared outcomes to 78 patients from the Management of Myelomeningocele Study and 100 in the post-Management of Myelomeningocele Study cohort, both of which used open fetal NTD repair by hysterotomy. Fetoscopic repair was associated with fewer cesarean deliveries (approximately 2/3rds vs. 100% in the two trials) and no cases of dehiscence or thinning in the uterine scar compared to 34% and 49%, respectively. There were no differences in need for treatment of hydrocephalus at 12 months.

Authors of the review cited above reporting on spina bifida repair over the 10-year period following the Management of Myelomeningocele Study Trial found mixed results from case series of fetoscopic surgery vs. open fetal surgery including higher rates of hydrocephalus (55% vs. 36.3%) but better rates of hindbrain herniation reversal (93.8% vs. 51.2%) and urinary continence (71.4% vs. 33.3%), although data are sparse. Fetoscopic surgery compared with prenatal open surgery was associated with increased rates of placental abruption (9.4% vs. 3.7%) and more cases of preterm premature rupture of membranes (63.2% vs. 30.7%).

In a retrospective cohort study of 146 fetuses with open NTDs comparing outcomes of 102 undergoing laparotomy-assisted fetoscopic repair (hybrid approach) vs. 44 undergoing open hysterotomy repair, the hybrid approach resulted in a significantly lower Clavien-Dindo Grade III complication rate (i.e., those requiring procedural intervention, but not life threatening: 4.9% vs 43.2%), a significantly lower overall comprehensive maternal complication index (8.7 vs 22.6) and a higher gestational age at delivery (38.1 vs 35.8 weeks).

Three-layer vs. single-layer closure during exteriorized uterus fetoscopic repair for open NTD may offer benefit of improved rates of CSF leakage and reversal of hindbrain herniation at 6 weeks postoperatively.

In an RCT of 40 babies undergoing surgery for meningomyelocele, the 20 patients receiving platelet-rich plasma (PRP) after surgical repair compared to those not receiving PRP had a significantly lower rate of CSF leakage (1 vs. 9) and partial skin necrosis (3 vs. 13) and none developed meningitis vs. 7 in the control group.

In a small RCT, a 12-week home-based, progressive treadmill training program for ambulatory children with spina bifida had a significant positive long-term effect on ambulation as measured by the 6-minute walk test.

Delivery of a child with an NTD should occur at a center capable of handling all aspects of treatment and potential neonatal complications, or termination of the pregnancy depending on the prognosis of the NTD and choice of the mother.

Data are insufficient to permit a general statement on preferred route of delivery. In a case series of 72 mother-infant pairs in a single institution, mode of delivery or avoidance of labor did not influence infant functional outcomes at 2 years.
Children should be delivered at term unless ventriculomegaly necessitates delivery prior to term for the purposes of ventricular shunt placement.
Anencephalic fetuses have no treatment other than comfort care if permitted to be delivered at term.

Urinary and bowel incontinence management and multidisciplinary care within tertiary care institutions have improved the survival and function of patients with meningomyelocele and encephalocele. A systematic review of retrospective cohort studies found that total continence was achieved in 38% of adults with myelomeningocele; outcomes were better with a lower level lesion and without hydrocephalus. About one in four had some degree of renal damage, with end-stage renal disease in 1.3%.

In one study, bladder abnormalities on urodynamic testing were more likely among adult patients confined to a wheelchair (OR 5.36) and were much less likely among adults with spinal dysraphism who were asymptomatic and not wheelchair bound.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 observational studies with 652 children with spina bifida-associated neurogenic bladder found benefit for proactive management (i.e., use of clean intermittent catheterization and/or anticholinergics by 1 year of age) vs. later start or no intervention for significantly lower risks of secondary vesicoureteral reflux (OR 0.4, 95% CI 0.2-0.7), non-febrile UTI (OR 0.4, 95% CI 0.2-0.6), and renal deterioration (OR 0.3, 95% CI 0.2-0.5).

In a study of 75 patients with neurogenic bladder requiring intermittent bladder catheterization, there was no difference in incidence of urinary tract infections between single-use polyvinylchloride catheters and reused (after washing with soap and water and storing in a container with 0.5% benzalkonium chloride) polyvinylchloride catheters (35.2% vs 36.8%, respectively).

Botulinum toxin type A injections are beneficial in patients with bladder hyperreflexia due to myelomeningocele; in a small RCT, injections in both sphincter and detrusor conferred additional benefit in decreasing postvoid residual volume and symptoms than intra-detrusor injections alone.

In one study, patients with myelomeningocele-induced refractory neurogenic detrusor overactivity had improved voiding symptoms and continence after transcutaneous interferential (IF) electrostimulation. In the treatment group, 78% patients gained continence immediately after IF therapy and 60% had persistent continence for 6 months. Rates of enuresis also significantly improved. Similarly, use of abdominal IF electrostimulation (3 times a week over 15 weeks) improved defecation frequency in one pilot study.

In an RCT of 34 adult patients with spina bifida and bowel dysfunction, those randomized to transanal irrigation had improved neurogenic bowel dysfunction scores and greater improvements in both bowel incontinence and constipation compared to those in the conservative bowel management group; overall improvement at week 10 was reported in 13 (76%) patients in the intervention group compared to 6 (43%) in the conservative group.
Children with spina bifida are at risk for low bone density and fractures.

The role of scoliosis surgery in patients with spina bifida appears limited to some benefit in seating. Hip reduction surgery for hip dislocation does not appear to improve walking B but may be appropriate in low-level unilateral dislocation.

In 2 retrospective chart reviews of kyphectomy for children with myelomeningocele, surgery improved kyphosis (average correction of 81%), and improved seating balance and skin ulceration; however, wound and skin complications were common and multiple surgeries were required in some patients.
Excellent prognosis for spina bifida occulta, with normal function and life span as the rule.B
With open spina bifida, prophylactic minimization of birth trauma, improved imaging techniques, and wide-spectrum antibiotics have improved prognosis for open spina bifida.

Rates of outpatient visits in a Canadian database study were higher among patients with spina bifida than for age-matched peers (2.9 and 2.2 times higher, respectively for youth and adults) as were hospital admission rates (19.4 and 12.4 times higher, respectively).

Risk factors for pressure ulcers in 603/3153 patients with spina bifida who reported ulcers at their most recent annual visit were: wheelchair use, urinary incontinence, shunt presence, above the knee orthopedic surgery, recent surgery, and male sex.
Meningocele has an excellent prognosis with proper identification and surgical closure of sinus tracts to prevent meningitis.B
Myelomeningocele and encephalocele have a fair prognosis with proper surgical closure and treatment from a multidisciplinary team of surgeons, therapists, and primary care physicians.B

In a long-term follow-up study of 84 adults with myelomeningocele, almost half (42%) had normal IQ and most (70%) did not require shunting. Forty-four percent were employed and 30% lived independently. Most to all used wheel chairs if the lesion was above S1 and all with lesions below walked. Fifty-four percent experienced decubitus ulcers resulting in 4 major extremity amputations.

In a substudy of 115 of the 183 women participating in the Management of Myelomeningocele Study, rates of clean intermittent catheterization use by 30 months of age were 38% and 51% in the prenatal and postnatal surgery group, respectively, this difference did not reach statistical significance.

In a median 10-year follow-up study of 42/54 children who underwent fetal myelomeningocele surgery, 33 (79%) were community ambulators, 3 (9%) were household ambulators, 6 (14%) were wheelchair dependent, and 26% had normal bladder function.

In a follow-up study of 161 children enrolled in the Management of Myelomeningocele Study, there was no significant difference between children randomized to prenatal vs. postnatal surgery in overall adaptive behavior or cognitive functioning at school age of 5.9-10.3 years. However, children undergoing prenatal surgery had improved mobility (without assistive devices in 29% vs. 11%, respectively) and independent functioning, fewer surgeries for shunt placement (49% vs. 85%) and revision, and higher parental ratings for quality of life and lower family impact scores.
Anencephaly: Terminal prognosis.B

In a case series of 63 pregnant women with uncorrected Chiari I malformation (congenital downward displacement of the posterior part of the cerebellum through the foramen magnum into the spinal canal which may be associated with neural tube defects) and 95 deliveries, there was no neurologic deterioration or signs of increased intracranial pressure regardless of mode of delivery or use of neuraxial anesthesia. Headaches were reported during 58 pregnancies, but there was no association between Chiari malformation size and headache incidence. Similar findings of safety of vaginal delivery and use of epidural anesthesia were reported in a case series of 21 women with Chiari malformation in the UK.

Women undergoing prior open maternal-fetal surgery for fetal myelomeningocele closure are at higher risk of uterine rupture during a subsequent delivery. In one retrospective case series of 77 subsequent pregnancies in 60 women, there were 5 uterine ruptures (9.6%) resulting in 2 fetal deaths. This is in contrast to uterine rupture rates among women with prior cesarean section which ranges from 0.2% to 1%.

In another retrospective cohort study of 72 mothers with prior open maternal-fetal spinal bifida repair, two of the 16 subsequent pregnancies were complicated by an open NTD, one pregnancy was complicated by a placenta accreta and one pregnancy was complicated by a uterine rupture, both with good neonatal outcomes. Importantly, almost half of respondents did not attempt to conceive because of their experience of the index pregnancy and caring for the index child with 75% of respondents reporting medium-term psychological problems such as anxiety and feelings of guilt.

tr.td: Spina bifida occulta
Midline defect of the vertebral bodies without protrusion of the spinal cord or meninges
Open spina bifida
Any neural tube defect other than spina bifida occulta
Meningocele
Herniation of the meninges through a defect in the posterior vertebral arches
Myelomeningocele
Herniation of both the meninges and the spinal cord through a defect in the posterior vertebral arches
Encephalocele
Herniation of the meninges and brain through a cranial defect
Anencephaly
Congenital absence of the cranial vault and cerebral hemispheres
Dermal sinus
A sinus lined with epidermis and skin appendages extending from the skin to the spinal cord
Tethered cord
Tissue attachment that limits movement of spinal cord
Syringomyelia
Progressive syndrome in which cavitation occurs in the central segments of the spinal cord, generally in the cervical region, with resulting neurologic defects
Diastematomyelia
Abnormal congenital division of the spinal cord by a bony spicule or fibrous band protruding from vertebral body, each half surrounded by a dural sac
Lipoma of conus medullaris and/or filum terminale
Slender, threadlike prolongation of the spinal cord from the conus medullaris to the back of the coccyx
